title: Graphs: traversal, spanning trees, shortest paths
kicker: ENCT 252 · Data Structure and Algorithms · Chapter 6
subtitle: Things and the links between them: maps, networks, dependencies.

sections.title: Graphs and how to store them
sections.body: A graph G = (V, E) has vertices and edges (directed or undirected, weighted or not). Store it as an adjacency matrix (an n×n table: O(1) edge test, O(n²) space — good for dense graphs) or an adjacency list (each vertex lists its neighbours: O(n + e) space — good for sparse graphs).

worked.why: A graph has 1000 vertices and 3000 edges.

questions.prompt: Which representation suits a sparse graph?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It stores only the edges that exist.

sections.title: BFS and DFS
sections.body: Breadth-first search uses a queue and visits vertices level by level — it finds the fewest-edge path in an unweighted graph. Depth-first search uses a stack (or recursion), dives as deep as it can, then backtracks; it is the basis of cycle detection and topological sort. Both run in O(n + e). On the small graph A–B, A–C, B–D, C–D, D–E from A, BFS visits A B C D E.

questions.prompt: Which data structure drives breadth-first search?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: First discovered is first explored, giving level order.

sections.title: Minimum spanning trees
sections.body: A spanning tree connects all n vertices with n−1 edges; the minimum one has least total weight. Kruskal: sort edges, take each unless it forms a cycle (union–find). Prim: grow one tree, always adding the cheapest edge leaving it. On the textbook graph both give total weight 37 (Prim 37).

questions.prompt: Why does Kruskal skip an edge whose ends are already connected?

choices.text: Adding it would create a cycle, which a tree cannot have.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A cycle means one edge is redundant.

figures.caption: Figure 6.3.1 — Kruskal
figures.note: Skipped edges would close a cycle.

problems.prompt: Find the MST weight of the graph in the figure.

sections.title: Shortest paths
sections.body: Dijkstra settles the nearest unsettled vertex and relaxes its edges (non-negative weights; O((n + e) log n) with a heap). Floyd–Warshall computes all-pairs shortest paths with three nested loops, O(n³): for each intermediate k, dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]). See the routing lesson in Computer Networks for the step-by-step picture of Dijkstra.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A settled vertex might later be reachable more cheaply through a negative edge.

sections.title: Topological sort and transitive closure
sections.body: In a directed acyclic graph a topological order lists vertices so every edge points forward — a valid order for building tasks that depend on one another. Repeatedly remove a vertex with no incoming edges (Kahn). For a>b, a>c, b>d, c>d one order is a b c d. Warshall’s algorithm computes reachability (transitive closure) with the same triple loop as Floyd using OR instead of min.

questions.prompt: A topological order exists only if the graph is…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A cycle would need every member to precede the others.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Lists for sparse, matrices for dense graphs.
  • BFS = queue, DFS = stack; MST by Kruskal or Prim; Dijkstra for non-negative weights.
